title: Reading Sprint Rail
user: An ADHD or dyslexic reader who wants to finish an article or EPUB chapter without losing their place, switching tabs, or separating notes from reading.

evidence.quote_or_summary: ReadAware’s author says existing readers are clunky and force people to wander between apps and lose attention rather than keeping reading support in one place.
A current 14-reaction request for configurable font family and size reinforces that reading presentation must adapt to the individual.

recurrence: The direct reading complaint and a current neurodiversity-first product both point to sustained demand; the cost is abandoned reading and fragmented notes.
current_workaround: Use a timer, hide apps manually, switch to paper, or use a generic read-later/reader app with notes elsewhere.
incumbents_and_gap: Reader Mode, Pocket, Readwise Reader, and speed-reader apps simplify content but do not combine a deliberately bounded reading rail, resumable place, and tiny local capture queue without feeds or engagement mechanics.
smallest_useful_product: An offline PWA that opens pasted text/EPUB, displays one adjustable paragraph rail with optional word highlight and scheduled micro-breaks, and saves one-line notes tied to location. Non-goals: social feeds, AI summaries, streaks, or diagnosis/treatment claims.
success_measure: In a two-week pilot, at least 60% of users complete five 15-minute reading sessions and resume the same document without manually finding their place.
monetization: one-time — the core value is an offline personal reading environment, with no reason to gate attention support behind a subscription.
constraints: Keep documents and notes on device; expose motion/reduced-animation and contrast controls; avoid medical efficacy claims and addictive streak design.
why_distinct: It is a deliberately low-stimulation session tool with location-linked notes, not a content recommendation or LLM reading wrapper.
